title: Demography and social learning impact norm misperception and belief revision following intervention
abstract: Abstract Misperception about prevailing norms, sometimes referred to as ‘pluralistic ignorance’, is a pervasive phenomenon, yet is largely unaddressed in cultural evolution scholarship. Focusing on gender norms, we used a two-stage experiment (n = 903 Americans) to test hypotheses about norm misperception and the role of social learning in correcting misperception. We hypothesized that reliance on outdated or limited social information would make older and less educated individuals most prone to perception errors. In contrast, norm misperception was greatest among younger and well-educated individuals, suggesting elevated exposure to misinformation. We then supplied participants with no feedback or identical estimates of others’ beliefs attributed to either an arbitrary source or to the majority opinion (priming conformity), adults over 40, or highly educated individuals (priming model-based social learning). Consistent with our hypotheses, social information improved accuracy in all treatment conditions relative to the no-feedback control. However, age and conformity cues produced the strongest updating, whereas the education-based prestige cue was indistinguishable from the arbitrary-source condition. These results demonstrate underappreciated variability in misperception dynamics and that, in this context, social learning privileges information from the majority and older, but not well-educated others. Implications for research on misinformation, cultural transmission, and intervention design are discussed.
